speechtext:
Talking about costs, the bill refers to the Canadian price in clause 11. That clause provides:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected on each barrel of crude oil exported from Canada-
Then, follows certain provisions imposing the tax to be applied to Canadian exports of oil. The only evidence that we have as to what the tax might be is in the statement made in the House by the Prime Minister on December 6 last. This is what he said, according to page 5 of the notes for remarks made by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons debate on petroleum policy on that date:
A characteristic common to all frontier oil, and oil from unconventional sources such as the tar sands, is that it is much more expensive to develop and to bring into production than wells in the southern parts of Canada. This simple, undisputed fact is often ignored because it contains an unpleasant truth. It means that the days of abundant, cheap energy for Canadians must come to an end. It means that the cost of producing domestic oil must go up before too long. It means that Canadians must be prepared sooner or later, in some way or another to pay for these additional costs or go without oil. Any attempt to hide these facts and to formulate future policies without taking them into account can only lead in the longer run to even greater shortages and hence to even higher prices than Canadians are now experiencing in eastern provinces. In short we must in the long run allow the price of domestically produced crude oil to rise forward a level high enough to ensure the development of the Alberta oil sands and other Canadian resources but not one bit higher.
Is that to be the Canadian price, or what will it be? The Syncrude economists engaged on the tar sand project estimate that the cost of production will likely be $10 a barrel. Is this the price that the Prime Minister talks about, or will it go as high as $14 a barrel, as it has in Venezuela? What charge is going to be added to the Canadian price so that this formula that will be applied by order in council will mean anything at all?
I should like also to refer to what the Prime Minister said on December 21 and December 30 when he was questioned by Bruce Phillips and Carol Taylor in regard to what action we might expect from the government. We ask the government questions every day and each day get a different answer. I am referring to page 8 of the transcript, where the Prime Minister said this:
January 3, 1974

I think here it's a question of perhaps not communicating the facts well. On the freeze we said quite frankly we'd changed our mind.
Both the leader of this party and the spokesman for the New Democratic Party have pointed out that when the freeze comes off we will want to know the Canadian price. The Prime Minister continued:
When we announced the freeze on the 4th of September it was till the end of January. That was before the Middle East war, before the Arab nations had decided to cut back drastically on their supplies. We were then fighting inflation and we said a freeze till the end of January will give us time to adjust. A month later, less than that, the Middle East war breaks out, energy becomes in short supply. It's no longer a question of fighting inflation. It's a question of making sure we have enough. So I say quite frankly, quite candidly on television, after a lot of agonizing thinking the government has come to the conclusion that we should extend the freeze. You can call it a contradiction. I prefer saying that the government has extended its policy. It felt that its first decision, made before the Middle East war, about which nobody could have any sure prediction, was a wrong prediction-
The question is, how long will the freeze stay on? The Prime Minister was then asked about supply, because he had said that this mechanism was really to guarantee supply. After being interrogated as to why his government had done nothing since 1967 to build the pipeline, he said this, as reported at the top of page 9 of the transcript of the interview:
I think the simplest and to me a telling answer to that, Bruce, is that on the 4th of September when I announced that we would extend the pipe line, Quebec said-never. We don't want to have to buy your bloody well western oil. You won't put a pipe line in here, or if you put a pipe line, we'll make sure that we send the oil in the other direction because we're getting cheap oil from the Middle East and we'll never accept this pipe line. So a stitch in time, for them even the 4th of September was not time.
In other words, the reason he did nothing about the problem, which has now become a crisis not only in Quebec but in the Maritimes, is that the government of Quebec had said "We don't want your bloody oil". I do not know whether to believe that or not, but that is what the Prime Minister said on television. Then, he went on to say this, and this is why I mention the point about consultation. Bruce Phillips said:
There are occasions when what provincial governments have to say to you about the energy question is not a point of view that you would necessarily accept.
I will not read all of the Prime Minister's reply, but he went on to say that we were going to build this such and such pipeline anyhow, whether Quebec wanted it or not. This is the kind of consultation the government has recommended this afternoon. It is the kind of consultation that the premier of Alberta, Mr. Lougheed, experienced, and it is the kind of consultation that the province of Quebec gets from the Prime Minister and his government.
I cannot accept for a moment that we are going to get consultation and common sense from the government, either through the Minister of Finance or through the Prime Minister.
Let me examine for a moment the history of this surtax since it was applied. The Alberta minister of resources visited Ottawa to discuss the problem of petroleum shortages. He had not reached home by plane before the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources double-crossed him and applied the first surtax. And the government talks about consultation! The government's consultation is like the old system that we used to read about but which I
Oil Export Tax
have never had tried out on me, though I have heard about it. It is like the mother and father who told son and daughter, when they were sick, to open their mouths and take cod liver oil whether they liked it or not. This is what I call the cod liver oil consultation method of the Liberal party, and it is the kind of consultation that the provinces are going to get.
I cannot believe for a moment that Mr. Lougheed-and I shall have something to say in a moment about Mr. Bla-keney-is going to come to this energy conference with the kind of goodwill that I am sure everyone would like to hope would prevail, since he has gone through this recent experience with consultation. The Prime Minister asked: "Well, when I was out in western Canada, in Calgary, why didn't the provinces then raise the question of a national oil policy?" Surely, the Prime Minister does not expect the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to sit down with him and plan a national oil policy for all of Canada. Yet this is the reply we are given. It is the sort of answer we receive when we ask whether there has been consultation and why the government does not have a policy. To summarize part of what I have said, I say that to give this government the power it wants to tax by order in council is to ask the Canadian people to accept in good grace what I would say is the greatest tax fraud ever perpetrated, not only on the Canadian people as the taxpayers but on the consumer using this energy in great quantities, whether at the individual consumer level or at the industrial level.
I started by saying I thought every member of parliament, whether he comes from western Canada, central Canada or the Maritimes, if he realizes his responsibility in coming to parliament, must speak in reference to the national interest. I was most interested to read today an article written by the Premier of Saskatchewan. I hope the government studies this article well before the meeting, because he has said some very important things.

speechtext:
Yes, everything is on the table all right, but nothing ever gets past the drafting board. Let me quote from what Mr. Blakeney said:
Some parts of Canada face a shortage of gasoline, heating fuel and other petroleum products this winter, and perhaps for several winters, and no one should pretend that this is not going to lead to hardships for some Canadians if nothing is done to protect them from a situation they did not cause.
That situation may or may not be serious, we don't know yet. But it can be met by well-considered joint action by the provincial and federal governments without resort to panic measures.
I think those are pretty reasonable words from the Premier of the province of Saskatchewan. He went on to state in this article:
9036

January 3, 1974
Oil Export Tax
We will face a much more serious problem in Canada if our major trading partners, particularly the United States, run into deep recession. Canada may be able to take some evasive action, but we could not escape the serious effects of such international events largely beyond our control.
There are parts of this nation where poverty has been an involuntary way of life. There are regions where many of the people, for generations, have struggled against adversity and have had few of the comforts and luxuries of our most prosperous regions.
I might say that this is true of the province of Saskatchewan in which I was born, and was also true of the province of Alberta in 1935 before a certain development took place. It was one of the provinces which did not default on interest payments on its bonds during the depression. That is the point Mr. Blakeney is making. He goes on to state:
Some people may not be able to afford to buy as much gasoline as they need for their cars. But they have cars.
Some people may lose their jobs, perhaps for many months, and this will be very hard on them and their families. But those jobs will return.
This crisis of inequality is the real national crisis we have to cope with. We are talking about large numbers of Canadians, quiet Canadians, who do not make headlines very often. Canadians who have been around for a long time.
He goes on to say that the real crisis is a crisis in respect of regional disparity at various points across this country, and he ends his article with a reference to the surtax provided by this bill:
Only oil, oil belonging to the people of Saskatchewan, should be sold on a different basis. It should be sold at a price, we are told, related to cost.
Now Saskatchewan doesn't object to the principle of selling essential commodities on a cost-plus basis. But why stop at oil? Indeed, why start with oil?
What about freight rates?
Western Canada was promised at the last conference that something would be done about freight rates, but all we have received has been information. Mr. Blakeney then asks:
What about freight rates? Lumber? Building supplies? Chemicals and fertilizer? Farm machinery? Automobiles?
Certainly, there is an inflationary price situation in respect of petroleum products which is working a hardship on those areas to which Mr. Blakeney and Mr. Lough-eed have referred, but we must realize that in the city of Toronto the value of a house today will be increased by $6,500 within a few months. We must remember that the price of lumber has gone up under this government by 200 per cent and that we have practically the highest interest rates we have had since confederation. We all realize there is real concern in the country.
Let me say to the government before I sit down that it had many years to make certain that energy could be transported to the various parts of Canada where it is needed at reasonable prices and with equity. The real problem today, whether we are dealing with oil, wheat or potash, relates to transportation. We cannot get the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to take action in respect of the railroads. This government has done nothing but vacillate and procrastinate as far as these problems are concerned. Our real crisis now is a crisis of government

resulting from the fact that this government is doing nothing and, as far as I can see, will do nothing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to make a few comments on this bill which I find most important like everybody else. I have spoken on Bill C-236 which is related to the present crisis and to the problem now facing us.
In our view, the government is introducing a measure that will give it rather extraordinary powers in matters of taxation on a natural resource, which is questionable all the same, from the point of view of provincial jurisdiction. The latter feel, of course, this is an encroachment upon their rights. It is for this reason perhaps that I would like to say a few words on this bill, considering the respect we owe to the provinces.

What concerns me as well as many others is to see that this bill that we are asked to pass in this House seems to be premeditated if one considers that we know full well that a federal-provincial conference of first ministers will soon be held. I have had the opportunity of referring to it two weeks ago. The bill now before us today prompts me also to urge that it be passed only after the conference.
We will be told, Mr. Speaker, that this piece of legislation is urgent, that we must act very fast in order to grant the government some powers that are said to be absolutely necessary.
We are also taking advantage of a temporary crisis and I suggest that this piece of legislation would give the government some extraordinary powers.
For the time being we know nothing about the wishes or desires of each province. One can be sure that the provinces are preparing right now briefs to be presented to the conference that will take place in a few weeks. We will know then where the provinces stand. It would be detrimental, it would be a mistake should this Parliament pass this bill quickly without knowing exactly where the provinces stand, their wishes and their desires.

We surely expect the producing provinces to be rewarded, we expect the profits of this tax to be distributed to them, but we do not know exactly where the other provinces stand. I believe that the right hon. Prime Minister gave us an excellent example of this on December 6, 1973, when he announced in the House, for the benefit of everyone, the action that the government was planning to take to reduce the difficulties that this crisis could bring to Canadians. Bill C-245 is precisely designed to permit the government to impose an export surtax of up to $4 per barrel. This bill would also permit controlling our oil exports. In his excellent speech, the minister stated this afternoon that already those $4 might be considered inadequate and that through an amendment they might be increased to $10. This bill also insures the sharing of the benefits drawn from this export surtax. A 50 per cent share for the producing provinces and a 50 per cent share for the federal government are put forward in the bill.
Without anticipating on the government's decision, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the adoption of measures to alleviate the difficulties of the Easterners is foreseen when one considers that 50 per cent share which will not be returned to the oil producing provinces.

In spite of all the presentations which have been made by the premiers of the Atlantic area, and in spite of all the presentations that have been made by members to your left in this House, Mr. Speaker, presentations on behalf of the Atlantic area, there is still nothing of any concrete nature which would suggest that there is relief in the offing for a new form of disparity which will exist in that area.

He indicates that the provinces themselves should do this. On one occasion he mentioned that the grants to the provinces had been increased and, therefore, they were quite capable of looking after any disparity which may exist.
This is totally unacceptable to the Atlantic area, and regardless of what those members from the Atlantic area who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, have said to their caucus, it is still not acceptable. Regardless of what the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) may have suggested, it is very obvious that there is very little significant influence or input, very little change in policy to be arranged by the presentation of the eastern Canadian problem as it presently exists in connection with the petroleum situation in which we find ourselves.
The unfortunate part of it is that all of the grants which have been made to the provincial governments have been made for equalization and other purposes. They may have been increased for the purposes of education, for the purposes of welfare, for the purposes of DREE, or for any

other purpose you may wish to mention. But as the grants were increased for one purpose or another this was only done in recognition of a problem which then existed.
I think the Prime Minister showed his total misunderstanding of the concept of grants from the federal treasury to the provinces when he suggested that the provinces should pick up the tab themselves, and that it was not the responsibility of the federal government. I say to hon. members opposite that they had better go back and review the synoptic report, or Hansard of this House, because the Prime Minister did say that the provinces should pick this up, and they were quite capable of doing so. Read his reply in response to the question posed by the hon. member for St. John's. Read it before some of the members of the Quebec government caucus allow the government to ride roughshod over eastern Canada, including Quebec. I say read it before you make your partisan, divisive speeches, like that of the last speaker, who accused everybody of division except himself, but who in his remarks showed he is sort of fuzzy in his comprehension of the whole problem, and used this occasion to attack others in a personal way. speechtext:
We are . not just making idle, idiotic remarks like some hon. members. We are not resorting purely to charge and countercharge across the House. Instead, we are pleading that the government change its course, and recognize the needs as they presently exist. The provinces of eastern Canada, including the province of Quebec, do not have the economic capacity to take up the difference in the cost of the operation of industry, of families, of automobiles, indeed of any facet of our lives.
How serious could this be, Mr. Speaker? It could be so serious that it would negate the effect of all the good intentions of the policies of governments, present and past, which recognized that Atlantic Canada, including part of Quebec, had to have certain special conditions if it were to share in the standard of life which was the objective of the government of the day. Now this is a new burden, a new inequity, which is hurting the economy of eastern Canada, including Quebec. We are being asked at this moment in time to say that this bill will cure the problem. The government has been saying, "Give us all the legislation we want with respect to energy, and we will cure the problem."
I would like the government to answer some questions. I would like it to tell us what the effect would be on the economy of the Atlantic area, what would be the effect on the pulp and paper industry, what would be the effect on the food industry, what would be the effect on all the industries of the Atlantic area which, for various reasons, may have been directed to the use of oil during the past 25 years because it was the cheapest possible source of energy and heating? Now, the increase in the price has reached such a degree that some companies, which have high energy requirements for the production of their goods and services, will find that the cost of fuel in certain instances exceeds the margin of profit which they enjoyed during the last five years.

As of December 15, the cost of home heating oil in the Atlantic area had already risen 60 per cent over a year ago. The cost of gasoline from the refinery, has virtually doubled and, depending on the tax structure, the motorist and the trucker in the Atlantic area have experienced a 30 per cent to 40 per cent increase in its cost. There is no longer any guaranteed source of supply in the Atlantic area. Consumers are discovering that their suppliers are saying they can supply them for the month of January, but then there is uncertainty, even though the National Energy Board has indicated that it can supply Maine with a little oil for its pulp and paper mills. But suppliers cannot see beyond January. As I say, supply in the Atlantic area is uncertain. The only thing certain is that the cost will keep going up.
The increases in costs which I have mentioned came into force before the last change in price. What a pleasant New Year's message it was to learn that Venezuela is going to increase the price of its oil by $4.80, or 80 per cent a barrel. The full impact of this increase is yet to come. What a nightmare for the Atlantic area to learn that the Middle East countries may raise their price as high as $17 per barrel. This means, of course, that Venezuela will follow. What does this do to the price of oil for the farmers, to diesel oil or gasoline? I do not think that we have to tell you that since fuel oil has already gone up by 30 per cent to 40 per cent or, rather, 60 per cent, the rise has just begun. There is no indication in anything said in this House today that any legislation, or regulations which may emanate from legislation will do anything whatsoever to relieve that price rise in Atlantic Canada when the full impact of the increases in the price of crude oil are felt.
The government shows a serious lack of understanding of the principles of confederation. Perhaps because I spent a number of years in a provincial legislature, I am aware of the diminishing responsibility of provincial governments as intrusions by the federal government follow one upon the other. If one has learned anything by observing this government in action for one year as of tomorrow, and perhaps by the day, one year today, it would be that its philosophy is that it cannot put up with the negotiation that is required in a democratic system; that it must establish for itself an autocracy and dictatorial authority; that it must put its power in the hands of boards which are not responsible to anybody. This is what it has done in this energy situation and is what it did in the foreign investment control structure. These things, sir, are not in tune with the creation of a united and harmonious Canada.
I am particularly concerned that this House has been asked to pass either of these bills relating to energy prior to the time that the provincial premiers meet with the government of Canada. This is a philosophical blunder; a complete lack of recognition of the authority, the pride and the responsibility that provincial governments should have, do have and would have if any other party in this House were the government. No other party in Canada has anything like the authoritarian complex and the dictatorial desires which are illustrated by the legislation we are being asked to pass today. This is a tragic situation, Mr. January 3, 1974

Speaker. It is this kind of system which brings disharmony. No matter what the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) might say, this is the kind of thing that irritates Canadians from coast to coast, to say nothing of the divisive statement, the personal attack ard the regional attack which that hon. member so unjustly and improperly mentioned in this House.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said that this government was going to administer a dose of castor oil to the provinces, whether they liked it or not, by the virtue of the authority which would be vested in them by this legislation. I might say that the castor oil they are going to give would not taste much worse or be more offensive than the lack of recognition which has been given to the Atlantic area up to this time.
The Atlantic area wants to know what this government is going to do to alleviate that cost increase. We want an answer to that question and we are entitled to an answer. What is the government going to do to assure the Atlantic area in particular of a supply of fuel oil? It has already stated that there is no visible physical capacity in Canada to transport oil from our present national supply to the Atlantic area or to the province of Quebec. What then are we going to do about price?
I am concerned about the remarks made by the minister today. But first, I wish to associate myself with my leader. I agree totally with what he said; I agree on the lack of clarity of policy and I agree on the lack of understanding of the Canadian problems. I feel very sorry for the people in the Atlantic area who get no understanding from this government, who get no sympathy from it; I feel very sorry for that part of Atlantic Canada which is represented by members on the government side of the House who have not had the courage to speak in defense of their own constituencies and their own communities.
I wonder what is going to happen, for instance, to the pulp and paper industry? Looking at the economic structure of that industry in the Atlantic area, it will be seen that the province of Newfoundland has found it necessary to take over a pulp mill. In many instances, in order to get further development, the provinces have had to find ways and means to support, subsidize or guarantee capital for the construction of new buildings and new production capacity. In these structures and in this production there is a massive consumption of petroleum products. If there is inflicted upon us a doubling, trebling or quadrupling of fuel costs, that industry which has been seriously hurt economically for the past ten years and is just getting on its feet, will receive a further serious setback. What does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) have in mind for this area? What does the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) have in mind for the farming industry?
In the last ten years, during the administration of this government, the farming industry has faced a trebling of labour costs and a doubling of mechanical costs. Apparently between now and the spring it will face roughly a threefold increase in fuel costs. What solution is the Minister of Agriculture going to offer to eastern agriculture to this problem? The industry is already hard pressed by viture of the massive increases in every other field concerned in the cost of production. What is going to be the
Oil Export Tax
continued effect of the various cost increases in fuel on food costs as eastern agriculture undertakes production for a price conscious consumer population?
I noticed with interest the other day that the cost of an acre of potatoes has increased almost threefold in the last ten years. This quadrupling of the price of fuel which we can apparently look forward to will be passed on to the farming community. The Atlantic area to a large degree has become dependent upon highway transport. Are the difficulties of this industry to be recognized? Will additional assistance in the transportation field be offered so that the trucking industry can carry on? This is a very serious situation and trucking firms are looking at their profit and loss sheets. They are looking at the rate structures and are finding that, with existing increases, they are in serious trouble. I suppose it is proper to say that firms in New Brunswick are not going to be in competition with firms in Alberta; therefore, the trucking industry is isolated in New Brunswick and you do not need to give it any special consideration. But we must remember, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of transportation always has been and always will be an integral part of the prosperity or lack of prosperity of the Atlantic region, and this is going to be a major cause of increases in transportation costs, as a large percentage of our goods are moved by truck. Even though presidents of trucking companies have been in contact with the government, and even though stock holders of trucking companies have been in contact with the government, they cannot get answers.
There is one question to which some truck owners would like an answer. I direct this question to the Minister of Finance, or to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce or to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). Are suppliers to be compelled to continue to supply the trucking industry, as they have been supplying them in the past year? Is the trucking industry to get any assurance that its fuel will be guaranteed and available, and is the government pressing suppliers to this end? I happen to know that one particular firm has received a virtual ultimatum from its supplier of quite some time. That ultimatum has been, "We don't know how long we can supply you, or if we will supply you at all". We have found that the price increases, as applying to some fuels, have been almost exorbitantly passed on to the trucking industry. This is particularly true in a case in which the trucking company may have sought a new supplier for reasons of price some time within the last 12 or 15 months. May we have assurances that this government will say today that as the trucking industry must be supplied with the necessary fuel, it will have priority. This assurance is particularly pertinent to the potato industry, which depends upon trucking for a large percentage of its deliveries to the Canadian market. If, perchance, we do not get that assurance, the lack of it may well impede the whole economy of the Saint John River Valley, which will suffer.
I heard a member from the other side of the House suggest that we, on this side, have no policy. If that were the case, I would have to say, after listening to the Minister of Finance introduce this bill today, that we are certainly in company with others who are no better off than

January 3, 1974

we are. Let me say that the only policy introduced in this House is one giving the government the right to control and to tax, without first explaining to the people of Canada exactly what will be the consequences and the effects of those actions. We do not know what is the grass root attitude towards the policy. What will be the effect upon Canada if the policy is implemented? What will be the benefit to Canada of the law, as enacted? What will be the opportunity for the provinces to state their case and obtain their just rights? There is no way to tell what the effects of the policy will be. As I said before, I am deeply disappointed that virtually all we have received has been the philosophical point of view regarding what might be done, what should be done and what can be done, but we have not been told emphatically or concretely what will be done.
We have been told that tens of millions of dollars will be collected weekly. We have not been told of what benefit this will be to Canada. The only benefit that would seem to accrue to Canada is this: more money will be brought into Canada, which in itself is a benefit as I acknowledge. But what is the rest of the benefit? There has not been associated with this tax and with this legislation any suggestion that we are going to seek oil, that we are going to facilitate the distribution of oil, that we are to facilitate the exploration for oil or that we are to harness the resources of Canada and try to relieve the situation in one year, two years or even six years. Nothing concrete has been put before us. There has been no suggestion of substituting one form of energy for another, or of developing new opportunities for energy. There has merely been a concentration of power in the hands of government, under a dark cloak, purely for the edification of the government. The government wants to say, "Look at how we are trying?" It does this so that its public relations people can tell all in this land of the importance of the legislation which it has brought forth. But, when members of the government are asked to expound the benefits of this legislation directly, area by area in Canada, they become as confused as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras). That hon. member showed that he has no concept of the general policy of his party, and he cannot put forward a policy for himself.
I was interested in listening to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle), who suggested that Quebec was being ill served by this legislation. He was another member from Quebec who said that the province is being ill served by the present policies of this government. His was a much more logical, proper and obvious approach for a Quebec member to take. I say to other members from Quebec that unless the government will implement some unknown factor which may be behind this legislation, Quebec will suffer with the Atlantic area. It will pay prices it cannot afford. Further, we are being led by a Prime Minister who comes from that province. He is selling the province down the river without considering the realities for eastern Canada. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-ALLOCATION OF FUNDS,-GRANT CRITERIA-REQUEST FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-ALLOCATION OF FUNDS,-GRANT CRITERIA-REQUEST FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr.Speaker, on November 9, as recorded at page 7697 of Hansard, I asked the following question of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras):
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. In light of apparent inequities in the allocation of LIP funds to constituencies, would he be prepared to ask the House for a reference to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration of the matter of the allocation by constituency of funds for LIP projects and the criteria which have been employed in making those allocations, and would he agree to appear before the committee and provide that committee with a list of the allocations made?
The minister replied to the effect that he would be appearing before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and would make that information known there. I then asked the minister the following question:
Can the minister assure us if he makes an appearance before the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee during consideration of the supplementary estimates of his department, that the figures, constituency by constituency, of the amounts of money and the criteria will be made available to the members of the committee and that his officials will be there to defend their position?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, that would be my intention. I point out that the expenditures under last year's Local Initiatives Program were made available in response to a question on the order paper, and that is what I would intend.
Since that time I have been looking for last year's expenditures, which the minister indicated would be made available. They were not made available at that time, nor were they made available later. Further, having looked at this year's allocations, I have done my very best to make heads or tails of the rationale behind them. I find it very strange that the bulk of the large grants to constituencies were made to those of Liberal cabinet ministers. I cannot claim that the allocations were made solely on political grounds because the smallest per capita grant in Manitoba was made to the constituency of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), a Liberal member. However, when you look at Winnipeg, Vancouver, northern Ontario or Toronto, you see that the second largest grants are almost invariably allocated to constituencies of Liberal cabinet ministers.
According to Manpower officials, funds were initially allocated to a province as a whole. That allocation was made in relation to the over-all unemployment figures of the provinces. They were made, roughly speaking, to the province as a whole, in the same proportions as in 1972-73. Within the province, statistics on unemployment and population were used to calculate allocations on the basis
January 3, 1974

of Canada Manpower areas. These allocation figures were in turn converted to a constituency base. They were then further modified to take in potential man hours of unemployment as proposed in the project submissions themselves. That is the official explanation of the officials of the Local Initiatives Program.
If the above explanation did indeed fully account for the methodology employed, then it is hardly likely that the constituency of Winnipeg South, that of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), would reasonably qualify for its accorded allocation either in terms of local employment rate or size of population as a percentage of provincial population or both. It is the second largest allocation in the province of Manitoba. The largest allocation of local initiative grants was made to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He represents the core area of Winnipeg where the largest population of the poor and under-privileged is located. That is just. However, the Minister of National Defence represents what is probably the richest constituency in the province.
I have attempted to convert the Canada Manpower Centre figures to the constituencies and that is impossible. I have attempted to convert the Department of Regional Economic Expansion designated and specified areas to constituencies and that is virtually impossible. subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-CHARGES AGAINST MEMBERS WORKING AT MALTON AIRPORT-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-CHARGES AGAINST MEMBERS WORKING AT MALTON AIRPORT-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 6 last I asked certain questions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in relation to problems that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police seemed to be having in connection with the taxi business at Toronto international airport. I have been in touch with the Minister of Transport about the matter on many occasions, but the matter has now become serious for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This is the police force that represents some of the highest ideals of Canadians and which is becoming involved in disciplining taxi drivers at the airport, creating an impossible situation for a police department to handle.
The problem results from a judgment of His Honour Judge Shapiro of the county court of the county of Peel given last year, as a result of which the authority of the town of Mississauga to licence taxis doing business at Toronto international airport was removed. As a result of this, if you, Mr. Speaker, were to decide tonight to drive to Toronto international airport, you, too, could become a taxi driver without being asked to take out a licence and would be able to pick up a fare. All you would need to do to operate legally is to put 25 cents into what is called the "spitter"; this would satisfy the Minister of Transport and you could pick up passengers. In addition, you could surcharge any fare as you felt was desirable, and it would not be necessary for you to have a meter. Nor would it be necessary for you to carry insurance on your vehicle. Indeed, it would not even be necessary for you to demonstrate that your vehicle was roadworthy. As I say, all you would need to do is to pay 25 cents to the "spitter"; you would then get in the lineup like anybody else. Of course, when you have people who are legitimate taxi drivers and have spent a great deal of money buying a licence and a proper vehicle, and anybody and his brother is allowed to get into the lineup, then you have a problem. The problem has arisen because of no licensing, no regulation and no control. People are cruising and picking up passengers.
The ROMP, who are trying to police the airport, have had an impossible situation to deal with. They have had to arrest and charge people who are trying to earn a living. The whole situation has become so serious that one member of parliament I can mention, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), has spoken to me about the problem he had in getting a cab at the airport. He told me he wanted to get over to the Cara Inn but could not get a cab because the fare was only a dollar or so; therefore he had to walk and carry his bag to the Cara Inn.
The Minister of Transport has refused to attempt realistically to regulate the taxi industry at Toronto international airport. In spite of pressure from the industry and repeated complaints not only by myself but by other members of this House, the minister has in effect abandoned his responsibility to police and to organize public transportation at the largest airport in this country. I suggest there is a hands-off policy or an "I don't care" policy. The result is that Charterway Service, which runs the limousine service at the airport, will probably very

soon, if it has not already, discontinue its entire limousine service at that airport.
The charges against the members of the RCMP to which I referred, and certainly there are not 90 as suggested by me in my question, have been laid by persons prosecuted. This has led to a situation in which the police are not even trying to enforce the inept regulations that do exist. It is high time the Minister of Transport took his responsibilities seriously and organized a system of licensing those persons allowed to use commercial vehicles to pick up passengers from this airport.
It is a disgrace that people who come to the city of Toronto to do business, or come as visitors, get taken to the cleaners by some hotshot people who pretend to be cab drivers operating rotten automobiles, without being licensed and without having reasonable metered fares. Surely, they should not have to accept this kind of service at an institution under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport. The minister has a responsibility to regulate the taxi service at this airport. He has no right to sit back and suggest that Toronto or the province should get organized. This airport belongs to the people of Canada and is under the control of the Minister of Transport, so this service should be regulated by him. It is not an excuse to put the RCMP in an impossible position, as has been done. There is a requirement on the minister to do something, and that is the reason I raised these questions on November 6 last.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-CHARGES AGAINST MEMBERS WORKING AT MALTON AIRPORT-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member put this question to me in the House on November 6, I told him I would investigate the situation and report to him. I did so by reporting to him in a detailed letter on November 16. Much of what I said to him then I will have to repeat tonight as not much has changed.
In his question on November 6, the hon. member said some 90 charges of assault and similar offences had been made by private individuals against members of the RCMP in connection with their work at Malton airport. When I investigated and reported on the matter on November 16, I indicated that during the last three years only four charges of any kind were preferred against members of the RCMP at Malton airport; one in 1972, which was dismissed, and three in 1973, one of which was dismissed and the two others were withdrawn. Since November 16, five additional charges of common assault were preferred against members of the force. Two of those charges were withdrawn, and three remain to be heard by the courts. One will be heard in January and two will be heard in March.
I must say that there is a difficulty existing between taxi cab drivers and members of the RCMP resulting from the enforcement of airport vehicle control regulations under the Government Property Traffic Act, and the government airport concession operations regulations under the Department of Transport Act. Enforcement activities in the main involve illegal solicitation of fares and illegal parking by taxi drivers at the Toronto International Airport.

In addition there is a conflict between the taxi cab owners and drivers and Airline Terminal Transport, which operates the limousine service, as to prime pickup designations at arrival and departure gates 1 and 2.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO- DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT FOR DEVELOPMENT-DEGREE OF CO-OPERATION BETWEEN GOVERNMENTS
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO- DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT FOR DEVELOPMENT-DEGREE OF CO-OPERATION BETWEEN GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) announced last May that officials of his department were meeting with officials of the provincial government to work out a general development agreement for northern Ontario. That meeting began on June 10, 1973. The minister expected to announce the specific program of industrial development for northern Ontario. In September 1973, I asked the minister in the House whether he was prepared to announce a strategy of industrial development for northern Ontario. The minister replied that in a few weeks he would make such an announcement. On October 29, 1973 I asked the minister once again the following question:
In view of the answer given by the minister in the House in September 1973, that an announcement would be made within a few weeks or a month with regard to development in northern Ontario, and since it is now, over a month, can the minister inform the House when he now intends to announce such a strategy?
This time the minister avoided answering the question by saying:
It is the working out of a general development agreement that is taking considerable time.
We are well aware of how long it takes for the government not to plan anything. In the meantime, the minister gratuitously announced that the current designations of regions and areas for purposes of the regional development incentives program had been extended to June 3, 1974. In the meantime, the minister continues to dole out, in a most haphazard fashion, a grant here, a grant there, so-called 'incentive' grants, which, for the most part, do nothing at all to alter the existing inequities borne by the workers and the small business people of the underdeveloped regions in this country. There is no apparent urgency felt by the DREE minister, or indeed by the government. There is no apparent pressing commitment to a fundamental restructuring of DREE. At best, its incentive program is as helpful as a straw to a drowning person and, at worst a travesty on the public purse.
Every announcement of change made by the minister is followed by another announcement postponing the previously announced change, which is then followed by another postponement, much in the manner of the one-step forward, two-steps backward routine that has characterized the Liberal Party, and the Conservative Party-

-throughout the history of this country. DREE follows the pattern of every other situation in Canada. Under the regional development program, the overdeveloped regions get the one-step forward, and the underdeveloped regions get stuck with the two-steps back-
January 3, 1974

ward. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was first seeking election in 1968 as Prime Minister, he declared publicly that there were two specific goals for Canada he was dedicated to accomplishing. One was national unity and the other was elimination of regional disparity.
Regional disparities were created and have been guaranteed by the lack of serious long-term planning and attention to the problems of remote or disadvantaged areas. There has been a dearth of ideas and well thought out possible solutions, and consequently a complete lack of productive adjustment to the DREE program. The Liberal and Conservative Parties have always found it easier to let things go until a crisis presents itself. That approach, that philosophy, reigns still, as DREE staff produce working papers that suggest, for instance, tourism as a solution to the problems of northern Ontario, when northern Ontario sits on, and mines, some of the richest ore bodies in the world. While the jobs produced by the minings of those ores go south and to countries all over the world, DREE suggests tourism for northern Ontario and slips in small incentive grants creating three jobs or four jobs or five jobs, and no fundamental change occurs.
If this government's success is to be gauged by the reduction of regional disparity between northern Ontario and southern Ontario, then it has failed miserably. Those of us who live in northern Ontario firmly believe that there is no excuse whatsoever for nickel plating plants, steel mills, wire factories and so on to be built in southern Ontario while our municipalities lack basic amenities or enjoy the highest taxes to provide such facilities. It boils down to simply a lack of sincerity on the part of those who govern to eliminate regional disparity in our neck of the woods. We are no closer to equality of industrial opportu-
Adjournment Debate
nity within our province than we were prior to the Trudeau years. Yes, time is running out on the Liberal Party in northern Ontario, and the sooner the better.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO- DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT FOR DEVELOPMENT-DEGREE OF CO-OPERATION BETWEEN GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) made it clear to the hon. member in his reply on October 29 that there had been excellent co-operation between officials of the province of Ontario and those of DREE throughout the detailed consultations carried out to develop the contents of a general development agreement with Ontario. The fact is that the process of consulting with the provincial government, and of discussing the policy thrusts that will govern the new regional development policy in Ontario, is a lengthy one. The hon. member will agree, I am sure, that full account must be taken of local opportunities and circumstances in this process to ensure that the developmental activities are tailored to the needs of the province and to the requirements of its slow growth regions.
I am pleased to assure the hon. member that the preparatory work on the general development agreement covering the development of Ontario and on subsidiary agreements to provide for the identification and pursuit of specific development opportunities is now in its final stages. I know that my colleague, the minister of DREE, will be pleased to inform the concerned members of this House as soon as the contents of the agreements are finalized.
